articles.title: 14 things you forgot happened in the NBA offseason, from Giannis and Jaylen Brown trades to Clippers' punishment
articles.summary: It was a busy summer in the NBA, with familiar faces in new places galore.
articles.body:
Chances are, if you're an NBA fan, you've heard about LeBron James' new team.

James' move to the 76ers was the headliner of a busy NBA offseason, with the league's all-time leading scorer departing the Lakers on a veteran's minimum contract to form an elite starting five in Philadelphia.

But even outside of James, it's been a long summer full of moves — since the Knicks were crowned champions in June, a collection of stars have changed teams, new coaches were hired, and major changes were announced for multiple franchises.

Here are 14 signings, trades, hires, and more you may have forgotten about from the past NBA offseason.

14 things you forgot happened in the NBA offseason

David Kirouac - IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

It may feel like Giannis Antetokounmpo has been a member of the Heat for a while, considering all of the news that has unfolded since then. But in early June, Antetokounmpo talks were dragging out more than ever.

After months-worth of speculation about whether or not the Bucks would move on, once they made real indications that they'd be trading their franchise star, two teams emerged as the favorite to land Antetokounmpo: the Celtics and Heat.

Boston was reportedly dangling Jaylen Brown in Antetokounmpo talks, but ultimately, Miami won the bidding war by sending Tyler Herro, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kasparash Jakcionis, the No. 13 pick, a 2030 first-round pick swap, unprotected first-round picks in 2031 and 2033 and a 2033 second-round pick to Milwaukee.

In the deal first reported on June 22, Antetokounmpo changed teams for the first time in his NBA career, and he now forms an elite big man duo with Bam Adebayo in South Beach.

There was a lot of hype surrounding the 2026 NBA rookie class thanks to a "Big Four" of sorts.

AJ Dybantsa, Darryn Peterson, Cameron Boozer and Caleb Wilson have all been viewed as potential future All-Stars, capable of becoming some of the best players in the league someday. Tanking has been one of the main issues in the NBA for a reason — a lot of teams were eyeing the young talent in this draft class.

Ultimately, the Wizards won the No. 1 pick at the draft lottery, followed by the Jazz , Grizzlies and Bulls .

Washington went with Dybantsa, who will pair up with Trae Young and Anthony Davis as a rookie, while Peterson joined an intriguing core in Utah, Boozer became the centerpiece of Memphis' rebuild and Wilson became the Bulls' next rising athletic star.

It's expected to be a thrilling race for the Rookie of the Year award this NBA season.

Victor Wembanyama lands lucrative extension

Part of the reason the Spurs were able to build a Finals-caliber roster around Victor Wembanyama so easily in recent years is that he's been playing on his rookie contract. The time came this summer, however, to finally pay him like one of the NBA's best players.

Wembanyama inked a five-year, $252 million rookie extension to remain in San Antonio for years to come — and he even passed on a potentially larger contract. Had he pushed for higher escalators, he could have made around $50 million more over the full extension, but Wembanyama instead took the 25% maximum over the 30% supermax escalators to $303 million.

The Spurs still had to pay a hefty price to retain the reigning Defensive Player of the Year, but they'll have some added flexibility to build around Wembanyama thanks to his decision.

Once the Celtics struck out on Antetokounmpo, it became the worst-kept secret in the league that they were ready to move on from Brown. But between his significant contract, some bad analytics numbers and their lack of leverage in talks, it also became clear that the asking price dropped more significantly than one would expect for a recent Finals MVP.

Despite rumors connecting him to the Trail Blazers and others, Brown was shockingly traded to Boston's longtime rival and the team it had just blown a 3-1 series lead to: the 76ers. On July 1, the teams agreed to swap Brown and Paul George, with Philadelphia also sending two first-round picks (2028, 2031) and two second-round selections (2028, 2030).

It marked a surprising end to a successful era for the Celtics led by Brown and Jayson Tatum, and also represented one of the more out-of-the-blue trades between rivals in sports history.

Ultimately, the Brown trade also allowed the 76ers to convince the free-agent market's big fish, James, to join the team on a minimum deal a few weeks later, completing one of the best offseasons in NBA history.

He's not the player he once was, but Klay Thompson is undoubtedly still a marksman. And after his Mavericks tenure didn't go as planned, with his numbers declining on a non-contender, he was able to reach a buyout agreement with Dallas.

Needing as much shooting as possible around Antetokounmpo and Adebayo, the Heat landed Thompson immediately, signing him to a two-year, $11.5 million contract.

A 36-year-old Thompson may not be the same all-around offensive threat he used to be, but he should get plenty of open looks from deep in Miami this season.

Ben Simmons returns to NBA before Achilles tear

For a while, it appeared Ben Simmons had played his last NBA game. With lingering back injuries and his struggles as a shooter, he fell out of favor in Philadelphia, Brooklyn and Los Angeles, becoming a free agent at the end of the 2024-25 season and never signing with a new team.

Simmons even began a professional fishing career, becoming the controlling operator of the South Florida Sails professional angling club — another sign that he was leaving basketball in the past.

But in early September, he made his official return to the league after a year off, signing with the Kings for $3.5 million. Simmons will likely never play a game this season, though.

In an unfortunate turn of events for the former All-Star, he is believed to have sustained a torn Achilles tendon at a practice just before the start of Sacramento's 2026-27 season, per Shams Charania . It will take yet another comeback for Simmons to get back on an NBA court.

Dusty May leaves Michigan to coach Mavericks

After leading Michigan to the national title in March and April, in a stunning turn of events, Wolverines head coach Dusty May decided to leave the program to become the Mavericks' replacement for Jason Kidd in June.

He became the first college coach to take an NBA job since 2019, deciding to take on the responsibility of coaching Cooper Flagg and a young core. May's Mavericks, not long after, drafted one of his former Michigan players in the first round: Morez Johnson Jr.

In May's absence, Mike Boynton Jr. was named interim head coach at Michigan.

NBA PROJECTED WIN TOTALS: Eastern Conference | Western Conference

One of many trades involving a former All-Star this offseason saw Grizzlies star Ja Morant sent to a rather interesting destination, joining a loaded Trail Blazers guard rotation now coached by Micah Nori.

At his peak, Morant was a high-flying guard in Memphis who led the franchise to playoff contention early in his NBA career. But over recent years, his relationship with the team appeared to have soured, including plenty of off-the-court issues.

The price to land the former All-Star was low — Portland flipped Jerami Grant and Kris Murray for Morant. Now, he'll begin a fresh start with the Trail Blazers, coming off a season in which he played just 20 games due to injuries.

If he can stay healthy, Morant will be one of the more interesting players to follow in 2026-27.

Tim Connelley has continually proven willing to make blockbuster moves to surround Anthony Edwards with premiere talent in Minnesota, from the Karl-Anthony Towns-Julius Randle trade to Rudy Gobert. This offseason, he did it again — but with a more out-of-line fit.

The Hornets decided to move on from LaMelo Ball after six seasons, trading him to Minnesota alongside Josh Green in exchange for Naz Reid and more. In the four-team deal, Ball formed a new-look backcourt with the Timberwolves, one that should, at the very least, be exciting on a nightly basis.

Ball's passing ability and 3-point shooting will add an element of shot creation next to Edwards he hasn't seen before. It appears to be a boom-or-bust move for Minnesota; if it works out, Ball and Edwards, paired with a strong defensive frontcourt, could lead one of the best teams in the West. But Ball has also dealt with inefficiency, decision-making and turnover issues often.

Nobody will blame the Timberwolves for not taking a chance, with some new energy behind them this season.

After the Lakers decided to part ways with James, they went for somewhat of a depth approach, signing a collection of role players in free agency to fill out J.J. Redick's rotation and surround Luka Doncic and Austin Reaves with defenders and shooters.

Quentin Grimes, Colin Sexton, Sandro Mamukelashvili and Matisse Thybulle are all new faces in Laker Land, but their biggest swing of the offseason was for a center. They went all-in on a big man who, on paper, would pair well with Doncic's passing skills.

Walker Kessler went from Utah to Los Angeles in exchange for two first-round picks and two first-round pick swaps, proceeding to sign a 4-year, $130 million contract as well. It was a pretty penny for the Lakers to pay — especially considering Kessler played just five games last season due to injuries — but he's also been one of the league's best rim-runners at his best.

In 2024-25, Kessler averaged 11.1 points, 12.2 rebounds and 2.4 blocks per game. He should blossom even more alongside Doncic's playmaking, now locked in as part of the Lakers' core.

NBA BOLD PREDICTIONS: Eastern Conference | Western Conference

Clippers hit with franchise-changing punishment for cap circumvention scandal, Kawhi Leonard traded

After almost a year, the NBA finally came to a conclusion in its investigation into the Kawhi Leonard-Aspiration scandal first unveiled by Pablo Torre prior to the 2025-26 season. And if you happened to miss it, it wasn't a good result for the Clippers.

In what was a historic penalty imposed on an NBA team, the Clippers were docked five consecutive first-round picks (2029-33) and fined $30 million, with owner Steve Ballmer, president of business operations Gillian Zucker and president of basketball operations Lawrence Frank all receiving varying suspensions. Leonard was fined $700,000, and his uncle and representative, Dennis Robertson, was banned for five years from conducting business with the NBA.

Initially, Ballmer indicated he would fight the penalties, but he and the Clippers backed down from that stance. Instead, they'll face significant challenges in building their team for years to come.

Another wrinkle of the punishment was that early in the offseason, the Clippers agreed to trade Leonard back to the Raptors, where he spent one season and won a championship in 2018-19 before signing with L.A. That deal was put on pause by the league until the results of the investigation.

Eventually, after the fallout of the scandal was official, Leonard was traded to the Raptors in exchange for Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick and five draft picks. For Toronto, it was an opportunity to add one someone who remains one of the NBA's best two-way players at age 35. For the Clippers, they added some talent and draft picks to begin a full-on rebuild with limited assets.

Leonard seemed to escape to greener pastures at the perfect time, re-united with the Raptors and forming an elite duo with Scottie Barnes. The Clippers, meanwhile, look like one of the weaker teams in the Western Conference, facing a far more uncertain future after the Aspiration scandal.

Just as the NBA was announcing the results of the Clippers scandal, the other Los Angeles team made significant news. Lakers owner Mark Walter agreed to sell the team to Josh Kushner and Bob Iger for a record valuation of $12.5 billion — just over a year after he purchased the franchise.

At the time of the sale, Walter was under federal investigation for alleged tax fraud, leading to some questions over any potential connections between the two, though there have not been any reports indicating that so far.

Walter also sold some of his other sports franchises, including Chelsea FC. He made around $2.5 billion in profit from the sale, originally purchasing the Lakers for $10 billion.

RANKING ALL 150 NBA STARTERS: 11-150 | Top 10

Jalen Duren ends stalemate with Pistons on $200 million deal

For a moment, Jalen Duren's restricted free agency appeared heading for a rough ending, unable to come to terms on a deal with the Pistons. Duren reportedly had concerns over a weight clause being added to the proposed extension, along with other issues throughout negotiations.

The Pistons center, named an All-Star for the first time last season, seemed to be considering picking up his qualifying option to become an unrestricted free agent next summer. Eventually, though, he and Detroit put their differences in the past.

Duren inked a five-year, $200 million extension that will make him one of the highest-paid centers in the NBA, locked in with the Pistons for years to come after the team showed reluctance to pay him as the No. 2 to Cade Cunningham.

NBA POWER RANKINGS IN 2029: Which teams have the brightest future?

There was never much doubt that Stephen Curry would be a Warrior for life, but with the team struggling to build around him over the last few years, there was always at least fan speculation that he could spend the final years of his career elsewhere. It doesn't appear that will be happening.

Curry, currently 38 years old, signed a two-year extension with Golden State worth $116 million, keeping him with the franchise through the 2028-29 season if he picks up his player option in 2028.

Not only will Curry remain one of the NBA's highest-paid players — he'll remain the focal point of the Warriors' roster through his age-40 season, at minimum. Any dreams from other fanbases of Curry firing away 3-pointers in another uniform appear to be dead, and Golden State will look to build one last title contender around Curry before he retires.

articles.title: “Coldest white boy I've ever seen” – Byron Scott thinks Cooper Flagg did not earn the right to be compared to Larry Bird
articles.summary: Byron Scott shuts down comparisons between the Mavericks star and Larry Legend.
articles.body:
Dallas Mavericks sophomore forward Cooper Flagg had a spectacular rookie season and many are already saying he will end up as one of the all-time greats. Some even took it a step further by comparing him to Boston Celtics legend Larry Bird .

However, former Los Angeles Lakers guard Byron Scott , who played against Bird in three different NBA Finals series during the 80s, is appalled at the comparisons. Scott says he doesn't see any similarity between Coop and Larry Legend, maybe at least not yet.

"The only thing that DeMarcus (Cousins) said that you know, Cooper Flagg has an edge is his jumping, his athletic ability. But that is not a skill. That's a god-given talent. He's able to jump higher than Larry Bird, right? But other than that, Cooper Flagg ain't got s–t on Larry Bird," said Scott. "I'm a tell you straight: Larry Bird still is, and I even hate saying it, the coldest white boy I've ever seen play basketball."

Too early to compare Coop to all-time greats

Flagg won Rookie of the Year honors this past season, averaging 21.0 points, 6.7 rebounds, 4.5 assists, and 1.2 steals per game. But Flagg didn't even make an All-NBA team while Bird was on the All-NBA First Team in each of his first nine years in the NBA.

Also, Larry Legend was one of only three players in NBA history to win the MVP award in three straight seasons. He also won two Finals MVP trophies while leading the Celtics to three NBA titles during the 80s, when they built a rivalry against Scott's Showtime Lakers. On the other hand, Flagg has yet to play a single playoff game.

"Don't start talking about Larry Bird and all the great white players who played. Don't do that. Let this man get 10 years in the league and then start looking back on his career and what's happened. But right now, the only other guy that even compares close to Larry is Pete Maravich. Cuz Pete Maravich was way ahead of his time. He's the only other person I would put in that category with Larry Bird," he added.

Maravich is the NCAA men's all-time scoring leader who averaged 44.2 points per game in his three seasons at LSU, scoring 3,667 total points during an era when the 3-point shot did not exist yet.

But more than his scoring ability, it was Pistol Pete's elite basketball IQ, court vision, creative passing and ability to make plays look effortless that made him similar to Larry Legend. However, despite being great as a player, Maravich's resume pales in comparison to Bird's, who was arguably the best player in the NBA from at least 1984 to 1986.

Unfortunately, Bird first injured his back during the 1985 offseason while shoveling crushed rock to build a driveway at his mother's house. Back injuries started hounding him after that and he ended up playing only 13 years in the NBA.

MJ called Bird the greatest forward to play the game

While Bird did not play long enough to set records and win more championships, the GOAT, Michael Jordan, once called the Celtics legend the best small forward to ever play the game and a Top 5 player of all time.

"People ask me all the time who my all-time five top players are," Jordan said in the book " When the Game Was Ours .". "And when I start saying Larry, they interrupt me. They say, 'You've got to be kidding me. He can't play with LeBron James!' I tell them, 'You guys don't get it. Larry is far better than any small forward who played the game, and to be honest, I'm still not sure if he is a small forward or a power forward.'"

No disrespect to Flagg and not to put pressure on him. But Scott is right, Bird is still in a league of his own and he has to do a lot more to be in the same sentence as him.

articles.title: Sixers' VJ Edgecombe on playing with LeBron James: 'He's exactly old enough to be my dad, which is crazy'
articles.summary: James finished his second NBA season before Edgecombe was born in 2005.
articles.body:
At 41 years old, LeBron James is the oldest player in the NBA as he begins his 24th season, his first with the Philadelphia 76ers.

While the league constantly replenishes with players who only played one year of college basketball, James is now facing players half his age — or maybe even less than half his age.

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Basketball league for the 2026-27 NBA season

For instance, Cooper Flagg — last season's NBA Rookie of the Year — is 19 years old and will turn 20 in December. AJ Dybantsa, this year's No. 1 overall pick in the NBA Draft , is just a bit younger, turning 20 next January.

Another of the league's youngest players is now a teammate. VJ Edgecombe turned 21 in July and is going into his second NBA season. He was the Sixers' 2025 first-round pick (No. 3 overall) after playing one season at Baylor.

Speaking to ESPN's Malika Andrews, Edgecombe acknowledged he didn't think he'd ever play in a game with James, let alone be on the same team with him.

"I ain't gonna lie, I thought he was going to retire like a few years ago," Edgecombe said. "So I'm like, 'Man, I'll never catch LeBron James in the NBA."' "He's exactly old enough to be my dad, which is crazy," he added. "His son is older than me, which is crazy."

"I ain't gonna lie, I thought he was going to retire like a few years ago," Edgecombe said. "So I'm like, 'Man, I'll never catch LeBron James in the NBA."'

"He's exactly old enough to be my dad, which is crazy," he added. "His son is older than me, which is crazy."

Edgecombe is right on that. Bronny James just turned 22 years old on Oct. 6 and is going into his third NBA season.

Even a more veteran teammate like Jaylen Brown was a child when James began his NBA career in 2003. Brown remembers growing up as a basketball fan watching and admiring the four-time MVP.

"The 12-year-old in me is, like, over the moon," he said. "No glaze, but you're playing with one of the greatest."

The Sixers announced on Monday that the team is picking up Edgecombe's $12.2 million option for next season . He also has a $15.4 million team option for the 2028-29 campaign. As a rookie, Edgecombe averaged 16 points, 5.6 rebounds, 4.2 assists and 1.4 steals per game while shooting 35% on 421 3-point attempts.

Philadelphia tips off the 2026-27 NBA season on Tuesday at Madison Square Garden against the defending champion New York Knicks.

articles.title: NBA Predictions 2026-27: Who will be champs? Our experts make their picks
articles.summary: Could we see a Finals rematch?
articles.body:
With the 2026-27 NBA season here, it's time to make our championship predictions. Who will win it all? Our writers make their picks.

Kelly Iko: New York Knicks. I have a gut feeling that some of New York's very public, very unfortunate and very off-court stuff could be a distraction, but this team hasn't changed too much and still has the wherewithal to go the distance. The other challengers — Raptors, Pacers, 76ers, Celtics, Pistons, Cavs — have too many questions in one department or the other. There's not a true hole on this Knicks roster or coaching staff, which is always the key.

Dan Devine: New York Knicks. I can't believe we've arrived at a place where I trust the Knicks more than any other team in the field, but we have. Yes, they've logged a ton of miles over the past two seasons, and yes, we're in an era where conference champions don't tend to repeat. But while I'm only guessing at the ceilings of the other Eastern contending hopefuls, I know how high a level the Knicks can hit. For now, that's enough.

Tom Haberstroh: Philadelphia 76ers. You can probably talk me into something like six different teams here. The East is absolutely loaded. So far, LeBron James and Joel Embiid are healthy. Until I hear otherwise on that health front, I'll go with the team with four All-NBA guys, a championship-winning head coach and sneaky depth.

Steve Jones: New York Knicks. The East will finally get respect this season. The competition will be stacked: The Knicks, Cavs and Pistons have continuity, the Sixers, Heat and Raptors made moves, the Celtics never leave, and Tyrese Haliburton is back! I believe the Sixers are absolutely built for the playoffs and am curious where their regular season adventure lands them, but I had the Knicks last year, changed the pick at the last minute to Cleveland (that got funny), and will not be doing that this year. Give me the Knicks building on their championship formula.

Nekias Duncan: Boston Celtics. There are plenty of great options to choose from, highlighted by the defending champs who lost [checks notes] one (1) player from their top-10 playoff rotation. I'm just a huge believer in what Boston has built structurally, headlined by an MVP-caliber talent in Jayson Tatum, who I think is primed for a huge year. They shoot, they rebound, they defend, they don't turn the ball over … they have my eye right now.

Duncan: Oklahoma City Thunder. That the Thunder dealt with as many injuries as they did and still managed to flirt with 70 wins and go seven in the Western Conference finals against an alien — while having a fourth-quarter lead! — is a testament to how great this team is. There's top-end talent to be excited about, internal development to bank on, elite coaching on the sidelines, and they should have a chip on their shoulder after how last season ended.

Haberstroh: San Antonio Spurs. A healthy Jalen Williams may have tilted the scales in OKC's favor last May, but I just can't shake how inconsequential Chet Holmgren looked against Wemby. I'm going with the still-rising Spurs.

Jones: San Antonio Spurs. The Spurs are going to have to deal with a different level of attention after surprising the league last year. But I feel like that, combined with an endless desire for revenge, ends up helping them out more than anything. They make it back to the Finals.

Devine: Oklahoma City Thunder. I'll take the Thunder, getting their lick back in a Western Conference finals rematch with the Spurs.

Iko: San Antonio Spurs. San Antonio has identified its mortal enemy, and nothing will take the Spurs off the collision course for a rematch.

Devine: Thunder over Knicks. New York takes the title defense as far as it can go before running out of gas, but Oklahoma City stakes its claim as the league's premier team, and SGA becomes one of just seven players ever with multiple regular-season and Finals MVPs, joining Michael Jordan, LeBron James, Tim Duncan, Magic Johnson, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Larry Bird. Pretty decent company.

Duncan: Thunder over Celtics. The star power of SGA and Tatum. The coaching battle of Mark Daigneault and Joe Mazzulla. The pageantry of a Paul George "revenge" series, and the bounceback campaign of Jalen Williams. Derrick White and Cason Wallace flying around. Alex Caruso and Hugo González also flying around. A fun, stylistic clash of the frontcourts — and plenty of screening goodness for nerds like me. I'd love every second of this. Ultimately, I think the Thunder are the best team in the league, and should be favored to add another title to the chamber.

Iko: Spurs over Knicks. We were treated to an absolute feast of a Finals a few months ago. Brilliant coaching, subtle in-game tweaks, star moments, press conference soundbites and more. Let's do this again, shall we? The only difference is I think San Antonio, now with Tobias Harris in tow and a new lineup look, has the tools to withstand the brilliance of Jalen Brunson, Karl-Anthony Towns, and OG Anunoby. (Sleeper prediction: A key member of this Knicks team gets traded by February.)

Jones: Spurs over Knicks. Who doesn't love a good rematch: The Knicks and their ability to poke at the Spurs' defensive rotations (and moving Wembanyama around the board), and the Spurs working to showcase an improved offensive attack and erase the memory of last year. It would be a blast, and I think the Spurs take it.

Haberstroh: Spurs over Sixers. Big Vic finally gets crowned as the champ. Rookie of the Year. All-Star in Year 2. Top 3 in MVP in Year 3. Champ in Year 4. Seems like a natural order of things. Only two other players in NBA history can claim that exact progression. Bob Pettit and Dave Cowens. It hasn't happened in over 50 years. Wemby is that dude.

articles.title: Angel Reese lifts Dream to first WNBA Finals win vs. Valkyries with historic breakout performance in Game 2: 'We feed off her energy'
articles.summary: The Atlanta Dream have yet to lose when Angel Reese hits a 3-pointer. She did that and more in Monday's Game 2 win.
articles.body:
SAN FRANCISCO — The sight, while more familiar this past month, is still an odd one. Angel Reese pulling up from the perimeter, her shot smoother by the game, an arc that drains through the net rather than short of it.

The Atlanta Dream have yet to lose when the third-year forward hits a 3-pointer, so when she took advantage of the space Kiah Stokes rarely allowed her, it served as the dagger, even if four minutes remained in the game. The 6-4 forward is 6 of 15 from 3 in the postseason after shooting 18 of 95 in her career.

The addition is a lavish accouterment to the standard fare she deployed to near perfection to even the WNBA Finals at 1-1.

Reese became the youngest player in WNBA history to score at least 30 points and 15 rebounds in a postseason game. The performance led the Dream to their first WNBA Finals victory in franchise history in a 79-65 win over the Golden State Valkyries in Game 2 at Chase Center on Monday. The series shifts to State Farm Arena in Atlanta for Game 3 on Wednesday, a tight turnaround after the contest was moved out of the Dream's Gateway Center Arena home.

Reese got her lick back after insisting the Dream's Game 1 letdown was the result of her not being aggressive enough, rather than anything the league-best Golden State defense did to quell her . The Dream, she felt, let one slip away in a 68-64 Game 1 loss in which she went without a field goal over the final three quarters. Looking back two days later, she said she became lax. It ate at her.

"We all came together and were pissed," Reese said. "We felt disappointed. We felt embarrassed and we didn't like the outcome of that last game."

So she changed it when she had the chance. Reese was the first player head coach Karl Smesko locked eyes with in the locker room. He saw what was to come.

"Oh, I like this look," he remembered thinking.

Stokes, who noted her increased aggression, surely didn't. Reese scored the first bucket of the game in transition, showing early that the Dream wouldn't be as stagnant as they were in Game 1. She had 8 points on 4 field goal attempts, 5 rebounds and 1 assist by the end of the first quarter. The Valkyries led 21-18.

The Dream found Reese on pick-and-rolls and pocket passes. They moved her around the floor. Stokes stymied her multiple times, joining Britney Griner (2014) as the only players in WNBA history with at least four blocks in consecutive WNBA Finals games. The center's presence altered Reese, who showed more patience in finding teammates. Her 15 points (6 of 9) and seven rebounds at the half led both teams on another paltry night from the floor (34% combined).

"Her rebounding, her fight, it was at a high, like, high level tonight," Golden State head coach Natalie Nakase said.

Atlanta (33.9%) lost every game in which it shot 37% or worse this season. It was 1% better than Game 1, but in a contest won at the margins, every bit matters for two defensive-minded groups. The bigger tell was Reese and Co. going back to ATL basics, bursting out of the locker room to tear the game to shreds in a 21-9 third quarter.

They sped the Valkyries up, feasting on cross-court passes and bad dishes out of the paint. Atlanta scored 12 points off of eight turnovers, nearly matching the first-half totals of each. Rhyne Howard's shooting slump continued, but her game-high six steals broke the WNBA record for most in a Finals game. The Valkyries couldn't get back in time, and allowed defensive lapses to compound.

"I genuinely believe that dictated the entire game when they can get more looks than we do," Valkyries guard Veronica Burton said.

The differentiator came at the free-throw line. Atlanta went a perfect 12 of 12, better than the 9 of 11 it shot in the first half. Golden State didn't attempt a single one after shooting a perfect 12 of 12 in the first half. Atlanta scored 14 more points at the line in the game.

"We're gonna see how close these actual fouls were," Nakase said. "They do lunge forward at times, and so we just got to make sure we take a close look."

The Valkyries are late-game warriors who can erase a 60-46 lead going into the fourth. They didn't. After falling behind by 21 with 6:06 to play, Reese's 3-pointer boosted the lead back to 19. Game 1 hadn't shifted more than single digits either way, and the first half of Game 2 didn't move more than six. The Dream led by four late in the second quarter, and entered the half up a bucket when DeWanna Bonner hit her first jumper of the day on the final possession.

There were 12 lead changes and 11 ties in the first half; only two each in the second.

It wasn't merely that Reese ratcheted up her offense in a series yearning for it. At times, she came out to the perimeter to guard Gabby Williams, her hero counterpart of Game 1 , limiting the veteran to 14 points on 15 attempts and zero late pushes. And by reigniting her engine, it reverberated.

"You can just see that [Reese] wants it really bad," point guard Jordin Canada said. "She's such a competitor, and we feed off of her energy. And so I think tonight she set the tone for sure, and it just trickled down through the whole team."

She created space for Canada to score 13 with 10 assists. Allisha Gray, playing through an injury to her shooting hand, scored 18 with three 3s. They could ride through Howard's two early fouls that quickly turned to four, and Reese's three at the half. She played the final 5:45 with five fouls.

"I let my team down last game not really contributing as much as I could in the second half [of Game 1]," Reese said. "Not even just about scoring, my screen quality, me hustling and wanting to get rebounds, and just doing the things that they know me to do. So I just wanted to make sure I came out tonight and left my mark and did whatever I could to get the win, and I think I did that tonight."

Atlanta's quest for a first championship in what is its fourth Finals appearance hinges on Reese staying this productive and, in her own descriptor, pissed. The first game showed they have a chance when she's quiet. The second proved their success is more comfortable when their offseason trade acquisition, dubbed a final piece of the puzzle, is her usual boisterous, aggressive, trash-talking self.

articles.title: Pepe Brasín señala al gran favorito al anillo de la NBA: "Es el año de San Antonio Spurs"
articles.standfirst: El periodista analizó en 'Las Brasas de Brasín' de 'La Tribu' el inicio de la temporada 2026-27, situó a Victor Wembanyama entre los grandes candidatos al MVP y repasó las expectativas de los españoles y los problemas del 'tanking'
articles.summary: El periodista analizó en 'Las Brasas de Brasín' de 'La Tribu' el inicio de la temporada 2026-27, situó a Victor Wembanyama entre los grandes candidatos al MVP y repasó las expectativas de los españoles y los problemas del 'tanking'
articles.body: La NBA vuelve a escena y Pepe Brasín tiene claro dónde pone sus ojos. El colaborador de La Tribu aprovechó sus habituales Brasas de Brasín para analizar el arranque de la temporada 2026-27 y señalar al equipo que considera mejor situado para conquistar el campeonato: San Antonio Spurs. Un pronóstico que pasa directamente por la figura de Victor Wembanyama, al que ve preparado para convertirse en la gran referencia del baloncesto mundial. “Creo que la sensación en torno a la NBA es que es el año de San Antonio Spurs”, aseguró Brasín. Y vinculó esa candidatura al crecimiento del francés: “Es el año de la llegada definitiva al estrellato, a ser el mejor jugador del mundo de Victor Wembanyama”. Brasín considera que el pívot francés está preparado para dominar la competición en diferentes apartados. Su pronóstico no se limita al rendimiento individual, sino que también alcanza a las aspiraciones colectivas de San Antonio. “Candidato MVP, candidato defensor del año, los máximos candidatos al anillo”, enumeró al hablar del escenario que imagina para los Spurs y su estrella. Eso sí, el periodista reconoció que la temporada tendrá que confirmar esas expectativas. “Por fortuna existe toda una temporada para descubrir todo eso”, matizó. También destacó otros alicientes del nuevo curso, como el cambio de equipo de LeBron James, el seguimiento a Philadelphia Sixers y la defensa del título de los New York Knicks. Para Brasín, la competición norteamericana tiene una virtud que explica buena parte de su atractivo: “La capacidad de generar historias, de generar capacidad de atracción de la NBA es casi infinita”. No todo fueron elogios. Brasín dedicó buena parte de su análisis al tanking, la estrategia de determinados equipos de priorizar sus opciones en el draft cuando pierden posibilidades de competir por objetivos deportivos. “Es un problema muy serio que tiene la NBA”, aseguró. Su principal crítica se dirige a las franquicias que, avanzada la temporada, dejan de perseguir las victorias: “Un tercio de la competición, allá por enero-febrero, decide que no quiere seguir jugando, que no quiere seguir compitiendo”. Tampoco le convence la modificación del sistema del draft con la que la liga pretende combatir esta práctica. “Han cambiado el formato del draft, yo diré que de manera bastante torpe. A mí no me gusta nada la variación que han hecho”, criticó. Brasín considera que repartir las opciones de conseguir el primer número entre más equipos no elimina el incentivo para perder partidos. “Competir sin necesidad de querer ganar partidos es una aberración y es un desastre para la NBA”, afirmó. Y no espera resultados inmediatos: “No cambian de la noche a la mañana, de un día para otro. Requiere mucho tiempo, requiere varios años”. El comienzo de temporada también ofrece motivos de interés para el baloncesto español. Brasín destacó la presencia de jóvenes como Aday Mara, Sergio de Larrea y Baba Miller, además de la progresión de otros jugadores que ya cuentan con experiencia en la liga. “Aday Mara es un jugador muy intrigante, mucho”, aseguró sobre el pívot, que afronta su etapa en Oklahoma City Thunder con la competencia de Chet Holmgren e Isaiah Hartenstein. El periodista cree que los problemas económicos que pueden surgir en la plantilla de los Thunder podrían abrirle oportunidades en el futuro. “No sé si para este mismo año, no sé si va a tener muchos minutos, pero creo que el objetivo de los Thunder es que Aday Mara sea importante en su futuro inmediato”, explicó. También habló de Hugo González, que podría ganar protagonismo en Boston, y de Santi Aldama, al que ve con posibilidades de encontrar su espacio en Dallas. Aunque todavía queda lejos la época de Pau y Marc Gasol, Brasín aprecia señales positivas: “No estamos como hace dos o tres años en cuanto al baloncesto español”. Entre el favoritismo de San Antonio, la irrupción de nuevos talentos y los interrogantes sobre la competitividad de la liga, Brasín celebra el regreso de una competición que le entusiasma. “Me encanta, me chifla”, reconoció sobre la NBA.

articles.title: Day 1 NBA Power Rankings, with Reasons for Hope and Despair for Every Team
articles.summary: The long wait is over.
articles.body:
We made it through the draft, the offseason, loads of trades and free-agency moves and the preseason. And now, the 2026-27 NBA season is here.

With opening night upon us, with all the information we could glean from all of the above, it's time to once again take stock of the entire league.

Based on the same criteria that have guided us for years—team and individual numbers, recent performance (so, in this case, the preseason), championship chances and plenty of subjectivity—this is how all 30 teams stack up right now.

ATL | BKN | BOS | CHA | CHI | CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GSW | HOU | IND | LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN | NOP | NYK | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX | POR | SAC | SAS | TOR | UTA | WAS

His shooting percentages have been ghastly in both the summer and preseason, but Los Angeles Clippers fans have to be thanking what few lucky stars they can still see for the lottery landing them Keaton Wagler before the league stripped them of five future first-round picks. The incoming rookie averaged 17.9 points and 4.2 assists, while shooting 39.7 percent from deep, as a freshman at Illinois last season.

Reason for Concern: The Past, Present and Future

Kawhi Leonard never played past the second round for L.A. The Paul George trade that helped bring Leonard to the Clippers depleted the team's trove of assets. And the NBA's salary-cap circumvention penalties cost the Clippers five more first-round picks. It could be a decade or more before fans are able to forget the painful results of the Kawhi era.

He has almost as many turnovers as assists in the preseason, and a point guard's field-goal attempts almost quadrupling his assists is a little concerning, but Darius Acuff Jr. looks like he could be an absolute blast to follow.

The Sacramento Kings aren't going to win a lot of games in the next couple years, but Acuff's heaters will ease the pain.

Reason for Concern: The Anti-Tanking Rules

Under the old draft lottery, Sacramento trading Zach LaVine and Domantas Sabonis would feel like a borderline lock. The Kings aren't going to be great with them, so it would've made sense to get some assets, move them along and get worse. But now, finishing with a bottom-three record gives you worse lottery odds than finishing with one of the fourth to 10th worst records.

Navigating that with a roster that's going to lose, with or without trying, will be tough.

Reason for Optimism: Better-than-Advertised Young Core

The Milwaukee Bucks almost certainly took a short-term step back when they traded Giannis Antetokounmpo, but 32 wins isn't exactly a high bar. And Tyler Herro, Jaime Jaquez Jr. and Myles Turner have all been on competitive teams. Herro and Jaquez could still be developing. There's plenty of upside with Brayden Burries and Kasparas Jakučionis, too.

The Bucks could be better than expected now, with plenty of room for future improvement.

Having said that, there isn't a single sure-fire future superstar on the roster. And Milwaukee fans got used to having that with Giannis over the last decade.

Even if they hit their relative ceilings, all the players listed above feel more like complementary players than alphas.

Final Record Predictions for Every NBA Team 🔮

Bold Predictions for 2026-27 NBA Season 🔮

NBA Stars with Most on the Line This Season 🫡

Reason for Optimism: The Young Backcourt

Michael Porter Jr. and Julius Randle are the players who might be able to keep the Brooklyn Nets out of the so-called "relegation zone" (where the bottom three records have worse lottery odds than the seven teams that finish ahead of them), but Mikel Brown Jr. and Egor Dëmin provide the hope for the future.

Both could be effective, high-volume three-point shooters who can also create for others. Pairing them could give Brooklyn a dynamic, unpredictable attack.

Minnesota Timberwolves coach Chris Finch recently told reporters , "We've traded moodiness for giddiness." He didn't single out Randle, instead describing Minnesota as a moody team in recent years.

For Brooklyn, the concern is whether Randle will take too many on-ball possessions away from Brown and Dëmin.

Caleb Wilson looked like a potential superstar at North Carolina, and that was based largely on his absurd vertical explosiveness. But in the Summer League and preseason, he's shown off some smooth wing skills. And as those continue to develop, he and Matas Buzelis could quickly become one of the most dynamic young forward duos in the NBA.

A lot of their early effectiveness will be determined by Josh Giddey, whose playmaking would benefit from defenses having to take his jump shot more seriously. He's had an above- average three-point percentage in each of the last two seasons, but defenders still generally play off him and try to crowd his passing lanes. If a more consistent Giddey jumper forces opponents to play him tighter, Wilson and Buzelis will get better looks around the rim.

Reason for Optimism: Stephen Curry and Yaxel Lendeborg

Even as he enters his age-38 campaign, Stephen Curry is still one of the best shows in the league. And this season, it looks like he may suddenly have a new, more dynamic point forward to play off of. Twenty-four-year-old rookie Yaxel Lendeborg looks like a seasoned vet this preseason, with averages of 23.7 points, 12.8 rebounds and 5.9 assists. And his team-first game should quickly jell with Curry's.

Reason for Concern: Injuries (or Illnesses) Galore

For those keeping track at home, Kristaps Porziņģis, Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody are all out indefinitely. There are no concrete timetables for the returns of any of them. And their salaries add up to almost $90 million and over 50 percent of the salary cap. Beyond that, Curry, Al Horford and Draymond Green are 38, 40 and 36, respectively. Durability isn't a given for any of them. And if Curry has an extended absence, this season could get real ugly, real fast.

There's plenty to like about the Memphis Grizzlies' young roster, but it's also not hard to settle on one individual player. In the Summer League and preseason, the skills that have made Cameron Boozer dominant at every previous level are translating. His "lack" of athleticism was overblown, and he's averaging 24.8 points, 10.1 rebounds and 6.0 assists per 75 possessions in these exhibition games.

Reason for Concern: Ty Jerome and Zach Edey's Health

Having said that, Boozer can't lead this team to competitiveness by himself. And Zach Edey (38.5 games per season for his career) and Ty Jerome (29 games per season over the last three years) have had a hard time staying on the floor. If those two and Boozer are together, the Grizzlies are going to surprise a lot of people. If not, they could be stuck outside the play-in.

The New Orleans Pelicans are a little like the late 2010s Orlando Magic. Like Aaron Gordon, Evan Fournier and Nikola Vučević, Zion Williamson, Trey Murphy III and Dejounte Murray are solid individual players you could imagine other teams wanting, but they just don't seem to fit together. And that could lead to a couple different potential outcomes:

Either it suddenly clicks, or they finally get some assets for some of the veterans.

Reason for Concern: No Face of the Franchise

Williamson is, ostensibly, the best player and face of this team, but he's often hurt, has yet to lead them to any playoff success and seems like a perennial fixture in trade rumors.

And while there are reasons to be intrigued by Derik Queen (his passing) and Jeremiah Fears (his fearlessness), it's hard to look at any member of the young core and see a guaranteed star right now.

Keyonte George and Ace Bailey are both worthy of a little hope. Lauri Markkanen and Jaren Jackson Jr., though older, certainly aren't past their primes. And if they can stay healthy, they'll make the Utah Jazz far more competitive. But the biggest reason to be optimistic about this team, without question, is Darryn Peterson, a smooth-moving 2-guard with real superstar potential. If he hits his ceiling, the Jazz could be pretty special in a few years. If he's better than expected right now, they might even challenge for a play-in spot in 2027.

Reason for Concern: Markkanen and JJJ's Health

Plenty of fans and analysts are understandably excited about the raw talent on this roster and Utah's expected pivot out of the rebuild, but the latter depends a lot on Markkanen and Jackson. If either or both miss significant time, fans may have to exercise a little patience. And for their careers, Markkanen has averaged just under 55 appearances per season, while JJJ is just under 57.

The Phoenix Suns may have been a little underestimated last season, but there's no doubt that first-year coach Jordan Ott also got the absolute most out of that roster that he possibly could. He helped make them one of the hardest-playing teams in the league, something that showed up in their opponents' turnover percentage and their own offensive rebounding percentage. And though the loss of Grayson Allen and Royce O'Neale may have cost them some of that grit, Ott will surely find a way to draw more out of everyone who's left (or joined up this offseason).

Reason for Concern: Top-End Talent after Devin Booker

Trading Allen and O'Neale for Miles Bridges was, presumably, an effort to address this concern, but after close to a decade in the league, it's pretty clear that Bridges just isn't a star. And bringing him in may have done little more than reduce the team's firepower from deep. That leaves a lot of pressure on Devin Booker to lead another "try-hard" roster to an above-.500 record.

The Washington Wizards are in a situation similar to Utah's. They have a couple of good veterans in Trae Young and Anthony Davis. They have a lot of young talent all over the roster. There's plenty of upside to be developed in Alex Sarr, Tre Johnson and Kyshawn George. But no Wizard can generate quite as much optimism as AJ Dybantsa, who looks like a dynamic point forward who can do a little bit of everything at a high level.

AD has famously struggled to be available throughout his career. And if he goes down for a long stretch this season, it could be harder to get back into play-in range than previously expected. Sarr has some potential and Deandre Ayton has plenty of experience, but the former still has a lot of growing to do on offense and the latter isn't a great defensive anchor.

After making his first All-Star team in 2025-26, Deni Avdija will certainly have the ball a little less this season, but that might actually be a good thing. Playing with Ja Morant and Damian Lillard should lead to more catch-and-shoot opportunities for Avdija, which should juice his scoring efficiency a little. And when he's on the floor with Lillard, specifically, defenses won't be able to crowd Avdija's drives as aggressively.

Reason for Concern: The Point Guard Logjam

New coach Micah Nori has already said it doesn't make a ton of sense to start Lillard and Morant together. The lack of size and defense between those two could be a problem, and they're not the only point guards Nori needs to find minutes for. Jrue Holiday and Scoot Henderson will almost certainly be in the rotation too. And while two or three of the above can ostensibly play some 2, that isn't likely to alleviate the defensive concerns.

We're still workshopping duo nicknames for Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving, but the pairing has a catchy ring to it, and their games should flow together just as well.

Flagg is already one of the most dangerous slashers in the league, and with Kyrie back in the lineup and dragging defenders out to the three-point line, the driving lanes should be wider than any Flagg found last season.

Reason for Concern: Dereck Lively's Health

Ideally, the Dallas Mavericks' high-end duo would be a trio. And when he's healthy, Dereck Lively II is talented enough to be included. But he's only appeared in 98 games in his three seasons, and he's still recovering from a foot surgery right now.

If he can get and stay healthy, the Mavericks could push for a play-in spot. If he remains a perennial injury risk, the ceiling is certainly lower.

Reason for Optimism: Three-Point Shooting

It remains to be seen whether the Charlotte Hornets can make up for the loss of LaMelo Ball's playmaking in the aggregate, but even without some of the looks Ball created, this team should make an absurd number of threes in 2026-27. They led the league in that category last season, are bringing back Kon Knueppel, Brandon Miller and Coby White and added Naz Reid, Royce O'Neale and Grayson Allen.

Reason for Concern: Lack of Shot Creation

The aforementioned loss of Ball could take more than this season to get over. His shot creation was a huge part of last season's success, and he was also second in the NBA (behind Knueppel) in total threes made. There's some untapped potential on the playmaking front from Knueppel, Miller and White, but Charlotte's offense was better with Ball on the floor in every season he played there (and it was dramatically better with him the last two years).

Jamahl Mosley did a good job of establishing a defensive culture during his time as the head coach of the Orlando Magic, but they never found a real offensive rhythm. Orlando had a below- average offensive rating in every season Mosley coached there. And while Sean Sweeney is a defensive-minded coach himself, there's a new staff in place that will overhaul the approach on the offensive end.

Over the last two seasons, Orlando is plus-9.0 points per 100 possessions when Franz Wagner, Paolo Banchero and Jalen Suggs are on the floor. The problem is that they've only logged 318 minutes as a trio in that stretch. Since the start of 2024-25, each has missed at least 46 games. The Magic may be good when they're healthy. There just isn't a ton of evidence to suggest they will be.

There's a good amount of young (or young-ish) talent still around that helped the Atlanta Hawks reach a mid-40s win total last season, but we sort of know who and what they are by now. It's the addition of a pair of championship-winning role players from the Oklahoma City Thunder that could drive this team to the next level. Neither Aaron Wiggins nor Luguentz Dort will have huge scoring roles for Atlanta, but the latter might start, and both bring tons of defensive know-how and experience.

Reason for Concern: Lack of Traditional Playmaking

Jalen Johnson's development into a bona fide point forward made it easier to trade Trae Young, but the team's offensive rating was only good (not great) when he was on the floor last season. And having a more traditional playmaker was helpful for Johnson's scoring too. Over the course of his career, he had a 59.9 true shooting percentage when sharing the floor with Young and a 56.6 true shooting percentage when playing without him. CJ McCollum, Nickeil Alexander-Walker, Dyson Daniels and maybe even Kingston Flemings can all take a little pressure off Johnson, but there aren't any dedicated, traditional playmakers in the rotation.

Reason for Optimism: The Return of Tyrese Haliburton

The last time Tyrese Haliburton was healthy and playing meaningful basketball for the Indiana Pacers, he'd hit three first-half triple-doubles and had his team leading Game 7 of the NBA Finals. It's now been well over a year since he ruptured his Achilles in that game and basketball fans (not just the ones in Indiana) should be thrilled to have him back. Haliburton is one of the best playmakers in the league, consistently and dramatically makes his teammates better and instantly makes the Pacers relevant again.

The biggest difference between these Pacers and the ones who made the Finals is Ivica Zubac now starting in Myles Turner's spot. That obviously means a lot less three-point shooting, which could make the middle of the floor a little more crowded for Haliburton's drives. Zubac is also a better rebounder, can occupy more space on the defensive end and is probably a better interior threat on offense, but there will definitely be an adjustment period.

For the most part, we've avoided established players in this space. And the Detroit Pistons do still have some intriguing young talent we could spotlight here (like Ausar Thompson). But Cade Cunningham is only 25 himself, and he just secured a first-team All-NBA nod.

Regardless of the drama that followed the Pistons (and Jalen Duren's restricted free agency) this offseason, they have one of the best young playmakers in the NBA. And even if an improved East will make it tough for Detroit to repeat last season's success, having Cunningham means it should be competitive for a while.

Reason for Concern: Lack of Three-Point Shooting

The two big deals the Pistons signed this summer were for Duren and Thompson, neither of whom shoots threes well and both of whom should start. Pair them with Cunningham, a below- average three-point shooter himself, and it starts to get real easy to imagine spacing problems for this offense.

Duncan Robinson and new additions Isaiah Joe and John Collins can help, but either or both of Thompson and Cunningham have to start knocking down long-range shots more consistently.

Over the last two seasons, Luka Dončić averaged almost 40 points and nine assists per 75 possessions when he was on the floor without LeBron James. And now, of course, all his minutes will be played without having to share the ball (and playmaking duties) with the legend. He's also heading into the season surrounded by solid shooters and finally has a rim-running big in Walker Kessler. Add Austin Reaves to all of the above, and it's easy to imagine the Los Angeles Lakers truly scoring at will.

L.A. may have a lot of 130-plus-point nights this season, but they're also going to give up that amount fairly regularly. JJ Redick has proven an effective defensive coach, but Luka and Reaves starting together is going to put a lot of pressure on Walker Kessler to clean up mistakes. And the frontcourt depth behind him, at least for the moment, is pretty thin.

Kawhi Leonard is back in a Toronto Raptors jersey. And assuming he's relatively healthy through the regular season and into the playoffs, Toronto will be a legitimate threat to represent the East in the Finals.

Leonard, Scottie Barnes and Collin Murray-Boyles give the Raptors one of the best defensive cores in the NBA.

Barnes has emerged as one of the most exciting young point forwards. And Leonard's one-on-one scoring will make the Raptors' attack far more dangerous, particularly when schemes break down at the end of games.

Reason for Concern: Three-Point Shooting

Leonard is a far more reliable shooter than the wing he's replacing (Brandon Ingram), but Toronto is still starting three players who command little to no attention outside the three-point line in Barnes, RJ Barrett and Jakob Poeltl.

In the playoffs, when defenses are more willing to ignore non-shooters, that can create some serious spacing problems.

Trading for Kevin Durant instantly oriented the Houston Rockets onto a win-now timeline, but it really shouldn't feel as urgent for them as it does for some other title contenders.

Reed Sheppard, Alperen Şengün, Jabari Smith Jr. and Amen Thompson are all 24 or younger and have star potential—or, in Şengün's case, have already reached that level.

There's enough veteran talent here to seriously threaten for a championship, but the younger players should keep them relevant beyond KD's departure or retirement.

Still, Durant's presence means Houston should want to win it all now . Pulling that off is heavily dependent on the veterans, almost all of whom have serious durability questions.

Durant has been remarkably healthy the last few years, but he is a 38-year-old forward with a torn Achilles in his history. Fred VanVleet is coming off a torn ACL.

Steven Adams has averaged 33 games per season over the last four. Bogdan Bogdanović is 34 and has appeared in 77 games in the last two seasons. And Marcus Smart hasn't played more than 62 games since 2021-22.

For years, the Cleveland Cavaliers have appeared to have things pretty well settled at both the guard and big spots. With James Harden and Donovan Mitchell in the backcourt and Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen inside, that's still true today. But there's long been a hole, or at least a mild concern, at the 3 in the middle of that lineup. They're certainly hoping to have it this year with Peyton Watson. And if he's the player he was from December 31 through February 1, when he averaged 22.5 points and shot 46.2 percent from deep, the Cavs could represent the East in the Finals.

Reason for Concern: James Harden's Playoff History

On balance, Harden has been a productive playoff player. He's 25th all time in career postseason box plus/minus , but there's no doubt that his lows are spectacularly low. Of his 191 playoff games, Harden has had a sub-10 game score in 45 of them. And in those 45 games, he's averaged 10.9 points and 4.0 assists, while shooting 28.0 percent from the field and 18.3 percent from deep.

Reason for Optimism: Back in the Superstar Business

The Miami Heat hit their organizational peaks with some of the biggest names in the sport on their rosters. And while Jimmy Butler certainly played like a superstar during some of his playoff runs with the Heat, Giannis Antetokounmpo is closer to the profile of the likes of LeBron James, Dwyane Wade and Shaquille O'Neal. And though he may be past his own absolute peak, he's still going to put up MVP-like numbers, when available. And if he's healthy in the spring and summer, the Heat could challenge for another championship.

Miami's front office did a good job of rounding out its rotation with good shooters. In addition to holdovers Davion Mitchell and Andrew Wiggins, Klay Thompson, Tim Hardaway Jr. and Bobby Portis all have the potential to shoot 40-plus percent from deep this season. But, barring a late-career shooting breakout from Bam Adebayo or Giannis, there's a pretty serious overlap in skills (and lack of shooting) between Miami's two best players. And that could bog the offense down a bit in key moments.

The Denver Nuggets were understandably panned for much of the offseason. After an embarrassing first-round loss to the Minnesota Timberwolves, they lost Peyton Watson—the one real shot at upside on the roster—in restricted free agency.

But adding DeMar DeRozan and Marvin Bagley III and hanging onto Spencer Jones gives Denver a second unit that may finally help it survive the non-Nikola Jokić minutes.

DeRozan's one-on-one skill is the key, but Tyus Jones' steady-handed playmaking, Spencer Jones' defense, Julian Strawther's confidence as a shooter and Bagley's finishing will all help.

Jokić is one of the most reliably available superstars of his era, but at this point, Jamal Murray, Aaron Gordon and Cameron Johnson all have to be considered pretty significant injury risks.

Gordon, in particular, has struggled to shake soft tissue injuries down the stretch. And if he's compromised in the postseason, Denver's chances at a second title will be almost nonexistent.

Years ago, when much of the league was still emphasizing versatility and small-ball, the Minnesota Timberwolves zagged, traded for Rudy Gobert and made multiple conference finals playing big. Now when much of the NBA is upsizing, Minnesota unloaded Julius Randle and Naz Reid and brought in LaMelo Ball. And after seeing just a handful of preseason possessions, it's already easy to get excited about the offensive potential of the Ball-Anthony Edwards backcourt. Both are among the most effective high-volume three-point shooters in the league. Ball is one of its best creators and passers. And Edwards will be perhaps the best finisher he's ever played with.

Minnesota's starting lineup, whether the fifth spot is occupied by Jonathan Kuminga or Ayo Dosunmu, is going to be one of the best groups in the league. But the talent behind it is largely unproven. Bones Hyland and the odd man out between Kuminga and Dosunmu will have their moments, but Terrence Shannon Jr. and Joan Beringer have a lot of growing to do before they're ready to be championship-level role players.

If you could somehow measure how much pure talent a team possesses, the Philadelphia 76ers would almost certainly be near the top of the league.

Tyrese Maxey and VJ Edgecombe make up one of the most dynamic backcourts the NBA has. Joel Embiid, when healthy, can still be a devastatingly effective scorer. Jaylen Brown is coming off a season in which he averaged a career-high 28.7 points.

And LeBron James, even in his age-42 season, can bring playmaking and know-how that ties it all together.

Health is a key consideration for plenty of teams around the league, but it's especially concerning for the Sixers.

Again, LeBron is about to turn 42. Embiid's struggles to stay on the floor have been discussed ad nauseam, and he lacked explosiveness at times in the preseason. If either or both are hurt in the playoffs, Philly's shot at a title will be at risk.

Reason for Optimism: The Potential Jaylen Brown Replacement(s)

Practically speaking, a healthy Jayson Tatum is the Boston Celtics' replacement for the 2025-26 version of Jaylen Brown. But for the Celtics to get back to championship level, they'll need someone to replace the pre-2025-26 version of Brown.

Actually, with the current roster, it'll probably have to be multiple someones. And with Paul George, Hugo González and Baylor Scheierman, Boston may be able to make up the production in the aggregate.

The Celtics have enough depth and are coached well enough to survive some absences in the regular season, but Tatum is coming off a ruptured Achilles, Paul George is oft-injured and 36 and Mitchell Robinson has his own troubles staying on the floor.

If one or more are gone in the playoffs, getting back to the mountaintop may be impossible.

Reason for Optimism: The Starters are Back

Over the course of the 2026 playoffs, the New York Knicks proved themselves to have one of the NBA's best starting lineups—if not the best.

Jalen Brunson's playmaking (for himself and others), Mikal Bridges and OG Anunoby's three-and-D contributions, Karl-Anthony Towns' shooting and rebounding, and Josh Hart's ability to fill in the gaps took New York all the way to a title.

The Knicks played most of the postseason with a seven- or eight-man rotation. Jordan Clarkson and Jose Alvarado appeared in most of the games, but they were both around 10 minutes per.

And over the offseason, they lost crucial offensive rebounder and big man Mitchell Robinson. Andre Drummond can replace some of what went out the door, but this team's depth will be tested in the 2027 postseason.

Reason for Optimism: This Is Just Getting Started

We've gotten over our skis on a number of young cores in recent years, but it's hard to imagine how this one can actually go wrong.

Victor Wembanyama, Stephon Castle and Dylan Harper are 22, 21 and 20, respectively. Wemby's already a "best in the world" contender. Castle had a fringe-of-the-fringes All-Star case last season. And Harper looked like the second-best Spur for prolonged stretches of the playoffs.

All three are several years away from their primes.

For a player with Wemby's slender, 7'4" frame, health is always going to be the primary concern. And to date, he's only averaged 60.3 appearances per year. He, of course, stayed upright during last year's Finals run, but if he's hurt down the stretch, San Antonio's title chances will be shot.

Reason for Optimism: The Mid-First-Round Picks

As if the Oklahoma City Thunder needed this kind of help, it looks like they may have landed a pair of keepers in the middle of the first round this past summer.

In just 23.3 minutes, Aday Mara averaged 13.4 points, 7.6 rebounds and 2.8 assists, while shooting 78.8 percent from the field. And Bennett Stirtz added 14.6 points and 3.0 assists in 27.2 minutes, while shooting 48.4 percent from deep.

He could realistically be a concern for every team in the NBA, but Victor Wembanyama is especially tough for the Thunder. He appears to have Chet Holmgren's number in a way that legitimately shakes OKC's young star. And his dominance over him predates their time in the NBA.

If the Thunder and San Antonio Spurs meet in the postseason again, Holmgren is going to have to discover a new approach to the matchup.

articles.title: La nueva armada española llama a la puerta de la NBA
articles.standfirst: Una generación plena de talento con cinco jugadores y dos aspirantes al anillo pide paso
articles.summary: Una generación plena de talento con cinco jugadores y dos aspirantes al anillo pide paso
articles.body: España vuelve a ganar peso en la NBA. La temporada 2026-27 arranca con cinco jugadores españoles, la cifra más alta de las tres últimas campañas, gracias a la llegada de Aday Mara (Oklahoma City Thunder), Sergio de Larrea (Dallas Mavericks) y Baba Miller (Los Angeles Clippers), que se unen a los ya asentados Santi Aldama (Dallas Mavericks) y Hugo González (Boston Celtics). Una generación con una edad media de apenas 21,6 años y cinco desafíos muy diferentes, desde pelear por el anillo hasta ganarse un sitio en la rotación. Con sus 2,21 metros y después de conquistar el título universitario con Michigan, el pívot aragonés de 21 años aterriza en los Oklahoma City Thunder, campeones en la 2024-25 y uno de los grandes aspirantes a una corona que ya ganó en 2025. Elegido en el número 12 del último 'draft', puede aportar centímetros, intimidación y una presencia interior que el equipo necesitará para competir contra los grandes pívots de la liga. Su pretemporada invita al optimismo. El reto será trasladar esas sensaciones a la competición oficial y ganarse minutos en una plantilla que aspira a todo. El segundo año suele marcar un antes y un después para los novatos, y el escolta madrileño de 1,98 m y 20 años lo afronta con una oportunidad para hacerse importante en los Boston Celtics. Su energía, su capacidad defensiva y su intensidad pueden convertirlo en un recurso valioso para Joe Mazzulla, pero necesita dar un paso adelante en el lanzamiento exterior para ampliar su influencia ofensiva. Si consigue asentarse en la rotación, podría participar en una nueva carrera por el título de una franquicia acostumbrada a competir al máximo nivel. Su primera temporada dejó destellos, aunque también una lección: no basta con prometer, hay que rendir cuando llegan los partidos decisivos. El ala-pívot canario de 2,13 m inicia su sexta campaña en la NBA con un nuevo destino y la posibilidad de convertirse en una pieza importante de los Mavericks. A sus 25 años, llega después de firmar sus mejores números en la liga: 14 puntos y 6,7 rebotes por encuentro en la temporada anterior. Su capacidad para abrir la pista con el tiro exterior y jugar en varias posiciones encaja con un proyecto que tiene en Cooper Flagg a su gran referencia de futuro. La incógnita está en su estado físico, después de los problemas de rodilla que limitaron su participación y le han impedido disputar la pretemporada. Si recupera su mejor versión, Dallas puede encontrar en él mucho más que un jugador de rotación. El base vallisoletano de 1,98 m llega a Dallas después de proclamarse campeón de la ACB con el Valencia Basket y ser elegido en el puesto 25 del 'draft'. A sus 20 años, su visión de juego, su tamaño para la posición y su capacidad para organizar el ataque le ofrecen argumentos para hacerse un hueco. La pretemporada ha reforzado sus opciones: ha promediado 9,5 puntos, 3,5 rebotes y cinco asistencias, con un notable 66,7% de acierto desde el triple. Sin embargo, la competencia en el perímetro de los Mavericks le obligará a aprovechar cada oportunidad. Su primera misión no será deslumbrar, sino demostrar que puede dirigir una segunda unidad y sobrevivir al exigente ritmo de la NBA. El alero balear de 2,09 m y 22 años, fue elegido en el puesto 36 del 'draft' por Los Angeles Clippers y aterriza en una franquicia que afronta una etapa de cambios. Su combinación de altura, movilidad, capacidad para rebotear y habilidad para conducir el balón le permite aspirar a convertirse en un interior moderno, capaz de defender lejos del aro y participar en la creación ofensiva. En la universidad de Cincinnati promedió 13 puntos, 10,3 rebotes y 3,7 asistencias en su última campaña. Su reto inmediato será trasladar esa versatilidad a una liga mucho más exigente y encontrar continuidad en la rotación angelina. El talento está ahí; el siguiente paso es convertirlo en minutos de calidad. La temporada dibuja dos escenarios especialmente atractivos para el baloncesto español. Mara puede tener la oportunidad de disputar el título desde su primer año, mientras que Hugo González aspira a consolidarse en un equipo con ambiciones de campeonato. Aldama busca estabilidad y protagonismo en Dallas, De Larrea necesita abrirse paso entre los bases y Miller quiere aprovechar el nuevo contexto de los Clippers. Ninguno tiene garantizado su papel, pero los cinco llegan a una NBA que ofrece espacio a perfiles muy distintos, desde el pívot dominante hasta el exterior capaz de cambiar el ritmo de un partido. El entrenador catalán afrontará su tercera temporada al frente de los Brooklyn Nets, una franquicia que también trabaja en la construcción de un proyecto competitivo. Su presencia amplía la huella española en la liga y confirma que el talento nacional no se limita a la pista. La referencia, sin embargo, sigue estando en los jugadores: cinco nombres, tres debutantes y una pregunta que acompañará al baloncesto español durante todo el curso. ¿Hasta dónde puede llegar esta nueva generación? En Oklahoma City y Boston, al menos, el horizonte del anillo no parece una quimera, aunque ganarse un sitio en el camino será el primer gran desafío.
